knowledge_point.title: Finding Particular Solutions of Differential Equations by First Rearranging and Then Separating

question.:question/problem: Find the particular solution to the differential equation $\operatorname{sin}⁡(x - 1)\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}-8(x - 1)\operatorname{sin}⁡(x - 1)=\operatorname{cos}⁡(x - 1)$ that satisfies $y(1 + \frac{\pi}{2})={\pi }^{2}.$ Assume that $0<(x - 1)<\pi .$
question.:question/worked-solution:
We first find the general solution and then apply the given initial condition to find a particular solution.

Separating variables and integrating both sides with respect to $x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(x - 1)\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}-8(x - 1)\operatorname{sin}⁡(x - 1) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(x - 1) \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(x - 1)\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(x - 1)+8(x - 1)\operatorname{sin}⁡(x - 1) \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(x - 1)}{\operatorname{sin}⁡(x - 1)}+8(x - 1) \\ \int \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x & =\int (\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(x - 1)}{\operatorname{sin}⁡(x - 1)}+8(x - 1))\,\text{d}x \\ \int \,\text{d}y & =\int \frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(x - 1)}{\operatorname{sin}⁡(x - 1)}\,\text{d}x+8\int (x - 1)\,\text{d}x \\ y & =\int \frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(x - 1)}{\operatorname{sin}⁡(x - 1)}\,\text{d}x+4{(x - 1)}^{2}+{C}_{1}.\end{aligned}
$$

To calculate the integral on the right-hand side of this equality, we use a substitution

$$
u=\operatorname{sin}⁡(x - 1)\,⟹\,\text{d}u=\operatorname{cos}⁡(x - 1)\,\text{d}x.
$$

Then  we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(x - 1)}{\operatorname{sin}⁡(x - 1)}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{\operatorname{sin}⁡(x - 1)}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(x - 1)\,\text{d}x) \\  & =\int \frac{1}{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡|u|+{C}_{2} \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{sin}⁡(x - 1))+{C}_{2},\end{aligned}
$$

where we used that $\operatorname{sin}⁡(x - 1)>0.$

Hence,

$$
y=\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{sin}⁡(x - 1))+4{(x - 1)}^{2}+C.
$$

where $C={C}_{1}+{C}_{2}$ is an arbitrary constant. 

We now apply the initial condition $y(1 + \frac{\pi}{2})={\pi }^{2}$ to find $C:$

$$
\begin{aligned}y(1 + \frac{\pi}{2}) & ={\pi }^{2} \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{sin}⁡\frac{\pi }{2})+4{\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right)}^{2}+C & ={\pi }^{2} \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡1+{\pi }^{2}+C & ={\pi }^{2} \\ C & =0\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus the particular solution of $\operatorname{sin}⁡(x - 1)\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}-8(x - 1)\operatorname{sin}⁡(x - 1)=\operatorname{cos}⁡(x - 1)$ that satisfies the condition $y(1 + \frac{\pi}{2})={\pi }^{2}$ is

$$
y=\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{sin}⁡(x - 1))+4{(x - 1)}^{2}.
$$

knowledge_point.title: Finding Particular Solutions of Differential Equations by First Rearranging and Then Separating

question.:question/problem: Find the particular solution to $\sin(x - 1)\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}-\left(10 x - 10\right)\sin(x - 1)=\cos(x - 1)$ that satisfies $y(1 + \frac{\pi}{2})=2 \pi^{2}$. Assume that $1<x<1 + \pi$.
question.:question/worked-solution:
We first rearrange and separate, then integrate and apply the initial condition.

$$
y'=\frac{\cos(x - 1)}{\sin(x - 1)}+10 x - 10.
$$

Use $v=\sin(x - 1)$, so $\mathrm{d}v=\cos(x - 1)\mathrm{d}x$. On the given interval, sine is positive. Thus

$$
\int\mathrm{d}y=\int\frac{\mathrm{d}v}{v}+\int \left(10 x - 10\right)\mathrm{d}x.
$$

$$
y=\ln(\sin(x - 1))+5 \left(x - 1\right)^{2}+C.
$$

At $x=1 + \frac{\pi}{2}$, $\sin(x - 1)=1$ and hence

$$
2 \pi^{2}=\frac{5 \pi^{2}}{4}+C,\qquad C=\frac{3 \pi^{2}}{4}.
$$

Therefore $y=5 \left(x - 1\right)^{2} + \ln{\left(\sin{\left(x - 1 \right)} \right)} + \frac{3 \pi^{2}}{4}$.

question.:question/worked-solution:
We first rearrange and separate, then integrate and apply the initial condition.

$$

$$

Use $v=\sin(x - 1)$, so $\mathrm{d}v=\cos(x - 1)\mathrm{d}x$. On the given interval, sine is positive. Thus

$$
\int\mathrm{d}y=\int\frac{\mathrm{d}v}{v}+\int \left(8 x - 8\right)\mathrm{d}x.
$$

$$
y=\ln(\sin(x - 1))+4 \left(x - 1\right)^{2}+C.
$$

At $x=1 + \frac{\pi}{2}$, $\sin(x - 1)=1$ and hence

$$
\pi^{2}=\pi^{2}+C,\qquad C=0.
